title: Caption Distillation for ReVision-Style Text-Only MLLM Pretraining: An Empirical Study

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to test whether content-aware sentence selection can mitigate the Long-Caption Paradox (longer captions hurting performance) in ReVision-style text-only multimodal large language model (MLLM) pretraining. None of the prior papers explicitly address this specific empirical relationship or test this hypothesis. While [1] discusses challenges with long captions in video captioning and [2], [14], and [24] explore length control in captioning, none of these papers investigate the Long-Caption Paradox or propose content-aware sentence selection as a mitigation strategy. Therefore, no prior work establishes the same empirical relationship.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves a systematic controlled micro-scale experiment comparing three conditions: (A) original long captions, (B) random length-matched selection, and (C) CLIP-scored caption distillation selecting visually relevant sentences by image-text similarity. [6] introduces CLIPScore as a metric for evaluating image-text alignment, and [8] explores using generated captions to improve dataset quality, including mixing strategies for raw and generated captions. [12] and [22] discuss image-text matching and similarity scoring, while [20] uses CLIP-based scoring for caption re-ranking. These works collectively cover the use of CLIP or similar image-text similarity scoring mechanisms, making the mechanism substantively equivalent.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design tests the hypothesis by comparing mean accuracy across three conditions (original long captions, random selection, and CLIP-scored selection). This design is a controlled comparison of conditions, which is a standard evaluation approach. [6] and [20] use CLIP-based scoring for evaluation, and [8] evaluates the impact of caption quality on dataset utility. These prior works employ similar evaluation designs (e.g., comparing conditions using CLIP-based metrics), even if applied to different objects or benchmarks. Thus, the evaluation design is covered.

### Domain
The domain is multimodal LLM pretraining, specifically focusing on text-only pretraining for vision-language models. This domain is well-covered by prior works such as [4], [8], [9], [10], [11], and [16], which all address multimodal pretraining or related tasks. While the specific instance of the Long-Caption Paradox is new, the general application area of multimodal LLM pretraining is not.

### Purpose:
The contribution's purpose is to explain mechanistically why sentence-level caption filtering fails despite preserving visually relevant content. None of the prior papers explicitly address this specific empirical relationship or failure mechanism. While some papers discuss related topics like object hallucination (e.g., [4], [6], [9], [13], [14]), they focus on hallucination issues or evaluation methods rather than the specific failure of sentence-level caption filtering to preserve object-presence mentions. Therefore, no prior paper establishes the same empirical relationship.

### Mechanism:
The mechanism involves analyzing what information sentence-level filtering discards, measured via object-presence benchmarks. Paper [4] introduces the POPE benchmark for evaluating object hallucination, which is directly relevant to the mechanism here. Paper [12] (RePOPE) also uses POPE to assess annotation errors, but it does not analyze sentence-level filtering. Paper [9] introduces NOPE, another benchmark for object hallucination, but it does not focus on filtering mechanisms. Paper [14] discusses object hallucination in image captioning but does not analyze filtering mechanisms. Thus, [4] covers the mechanism via its use of POPE for object-presence evaluation.

### Evaluation:
The evaluation facet uses the POPE benchmark to show that sentence-level filtering loses object-presence mentions, evidenced by POPE recall dropping from 98% to 88%. Paper [4] introduces the POPE benchmark and uses it to evaluate object hallucination, which matches the evaluation design. Paper [12] (RePOPE) also uses POPE but focuses on annotation errors rather than filtering effects. Since the evaluation design (POPE benchmark) is reused, this facet is covered by [4].

### Domain:
The domain is multimodal LLM pretraining. Papers [1], [3], [5], [7], [8], [10], [17], and [27] all work in multimodal LLM pretraining or related areas like multimodal retrieval, captioning, or generative pretraining. For example, [1] and [3] discuss multimodal pretraining frameworks, [5] focuses on hierarchical multimodal pretraining, and [7] explores multimodal pretraining for GPT models. These papers collectively cover the general application area of multimodal LLM pretraining, even if they do not address sentence-level caption filtering specifically. Therefore, the domain is covered.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to direct future work toward an approach that could preserve information lost by filtering methods. None of the prior papers explicitly report or establish this same empirical relationship or insight. While several papers discuss sentence compression or summarization techniques ([1], [2], [4], [5], [12], [19]), they focus on improving summarization or compression quality rather than identifying or addressing the specific issue of information loss due to filtering. No prior paper explicitly establishes the relationship between filtering and information loss or suggests future directions to mitigate it.

### Mechanism
The mechanism derives the suggestion that caption condensation (rewriting to preserve information in fewer words) may succeed where sentence filtering fails. Papers [1], [4], [5], [12], and [19] discuss sentence compression techniques, including rewriting sentences to preserve meaning while reducing length. For example, [4] generalizes sentence compression to include rewriting operations like substitution, reordering, and insertion, which align with the idea of condensation. Similarly, [12] and [19] explore compression methods aimed at preserving essential information. These mechanisms are substantively equivalent to the proposed caption condensation approach.

### Evaluation
The evaluation is presented as an actionable insight derived from a negative result, not experimentally validated. Since no experimental validation is performed, the evaluation design itself is absent. None of the prior papers rely solely on actionable insights derived from failure analysis without experimental validation. Therefore, the evaluation facet is uncovered.

### Domain
The domain is multimodal LLM pretraining. Papers [3], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [23], and [31] address multimodal LLM pretraining or related applications, such as vision-language models, image captioning, and multimodal retrieval. For example, [3] and [8] discuss the development and application of multimodal pretraining models, while [9] and [10] focus on pretraining strategies for multimodal tasks. These papers operate in the same general application area, making the domain facet covered.
